articles.title: Could life exist on Venus? Peptides survive harsh acid.
articles.description: The planet Venus is arguably the most mischievous planetary body in the solar system. This is because like Saturn’s largest moon, Titan, Venus is shrouded in a thick atmosphere that can’t be viewed with optical telescopes and require radar images to see the surface. Unlike Titan, whose atmosphere looks quite dull, Venus’s swirling and awe-inspiring clouds give observers the impression that its surface is covered in wonderous features. However, the truth is far from ideal, as Venus’s surface is a living hell with searing temperatures and crushing pressures. But, unlike its surface and Titan, Venus’s atmosphere provides many more ideal conditions, even Earth-like conditions. But while life would be hard to exist on its surface, could we find life in the atmospheric clouds of Venus?

articles.title: AI could undermine managers' judgment unless used carefully, study warns
articles.description: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) has become a routine part of working life, but overreliance on the technology may erode managers' ability to build moral insights, contextual understanding and know-how to get a job done, according to a new study from the University of Bath.

articles.description: Dark matter is an invisible substance that is said to bind the universe; scientists may have found new signs of it.

articles.title: Newly reviewed: Robert Ris' FritzTrainers on openings, calculation and strategic thinking (Part 1)
articles.description: Calculating variations, assessing positions accurately and finding the best move at the critical moment: few aspects of practical chess pose a greater challenge to players than concrete calculation. Robert Ris first addressed this topic in his 2018 Fritz Trainer, "Calculation Training", laying the foundations for a series of further courses. Lukas Koepl has taken a closer look at the various training programmes and, in this multipart overview, explains the main focus of each course and who they are particularly suited to.

articles.title: The five personality traits you have that scientists can tell before you're born... including some linked to PSYCHOPATHS
articles.description: Scientists have discovered over 1,200 genes which can tell if you may be at risk for mental illness in the future.

articles.title: Quantum oscillations defy expectations in this exotic material
articles.description: Scientists have uncovered an unusual form of electron behavior in zirconium pentatelluride, a quantum material that can act as both an insulator and a conductor. Under temperatures near absolute zero and magnetic fields reaching 60 tesla, electrons produced quantum oscillations that continued even after conventional physics predicted they should disappear.

articles.description: U.S. Senate candidates Karishma Manzur and Chris Pappas share they would support efforts to develop lithium oxide mining in New Hampshire.

articles.description: Researchers switched off superconductivity in magic-angle graphene by weakening electron interactions at distances as small as 0.3 nm.

articles.description: Researchers compared two superconductors under identical radiation conditions, revealing a sharp difference in their structural stability.

articles.description: During the most recent Ice Age, researchers believe there was a "lost land bridge" between Wales and Ireland.

articles.title: A new type of LED light could bring significant efficiency gains
articles.description: Researchers at Lund University have developed a new type of light-emitting diode based on thin, branched nanowires that could offer significantly higher efficiency and lower production costs than current technology. By controlling where in the structure the light is generated, the researchers have reduced the losses that would otherwise limit the amount of light that can be used. Their study is published in the journal Nano Research.

articles.title: In ant nervous systems, gene expression may drive rescue behavior
articles.description: Why do some ants help nestmates in distress while others don't? A research team from Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) and Tel Aviv University addressed this question in a new study. The researchers examined worker ants of the species Cataglyphis niger, some of which had shown rescue behavior while others had not. The results, recently published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, suggest that the key difference lies not in body size, morphology or the animals' energy reserves, but in gene activity in the nervous system.

articles.title: The DESI Legacy Imaging Survey Releases the Largest 2-D Map of the Universe
articles.description: The newest DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys map covers three-quarters of the sky and catalogs nearly four billion objects. This publicly-available database contains stars, galaxies, supernovae, gravitational lenses, and much more.

articles.title: Magic-angle graphene provides evidence for unconventional superconductivity
articles.description: Researchers have completely suppressed superconductivity in magic-angle graphene by screening interactions between electrons, helping resolve a long-running debate about the origin of the phenomenon.

articles.title: Health funds launch flu vaccination campaigns as supplies gradually reach clinics
articles.description: Health officials are urging the public to get vaccinated early, warning of high infection rates among children and the risk of complications.

articles.title: New AI tool maps the hidden universe of small molecules
articles.description: The human body and its gut microbiome produce thousands of small molecules that shape how the body functions—influencing immunity, metabolism and more. Identifying what those molecules actually are has been one of the biomedical sciences' most persistent bottlenecks. More than 80% of compounds detected in a typical biological sample cannot be matched to any known structure using current methods.

articles.title: Embedded platinum channels bring nanoscale spin-based thermoelectric conversion to bulk materials
articles.description: A joint research team from NIMS and the University of Tokyo has developed a new composite in which three-dimensional nano-interfaces are distributed throughout the material by coating the surfaces of magnetic-insulator powders with a metal and sintering them. Using this structure, the team succeeded in observing thermoelectric conversion driven by spins in an insulator, a phenomenon previously observed only at nanoscale thin-film interfaces, in a macroscale material.

articles.title: Food and water stations for wild birds are contributing to spread of deadly diseases, study finds
articles.description: Feeding stations providing food and water for wild birds are contributing to the spread of disease-causing parasites among farmland birds, researchers have said, with birds three times more likely to catch a parasite from these resources.

articles.title: Students with lower grades earn degrees more often when they belong to an academic major's majority group
articles.description: Despite efforts to encourage broader participation, women earn about 25% of undergraduate engineering degrees and 18% of undergraduate computer science degrees—and men remain a small minority among people earning nursing and education degrees.

articles.description: NANO Nuclear and Enveniam will explore US microreactor deployment, HALEU transport, fuel infrastructure and manufacturing.

articles.title: Same-sex marriages surged before Bolsonaro took office, Brazil data reveal
articles.description: A new study has shown that the election of Jair Bolsonaro, known for his homophobic views, as president of Brazil in 2018 caused a temporary surge in the number of same-sex marriages. The increase was particularly high in Brazilian municipalities where a large number of voters had previously voted for Bolsonaro.

articles.title: Virus-like particles enable gene activity tracking over time in the same cells
articles.description: In recent years, scientists have developed methods to measure a cell's transcriptome, or all the RNA produced by a cell, to study the cell's identity and genetic activity. However, these methods rely on killing the cell to access the bits of RNA within and offer only a one-time snapshot.

articles.description: Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have developed a fast, simple way to turn lignin, a plentiful plant-based byproduct of the papermaking industry, into potentially more valuable renewable chemicals.

articles.title: In a first, scientists identify origin of ‘beating’ signal hidden in quantum material
articles.description: Researchers have solved the years-long mystery about the origins of the ‘beating’ signal in the topological insulator (TI) nanowires.

articles.title: AI-driven polymer discovery could replace years of trial and error with closed-loop testing
articles.description: In the realm of materials science, there is a plethora of datasets and tools at our disposal—the issue is how to effectively use these resources in harmony. Researchers at the Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), Tohoku University, have identified major bottlenecks holding back artificial intelligence-driven polymer innovation and created a system that integrates multiple tools (such as polymer databases, predictive models, AI agents and automated laboratories).

articles.title: AI helps dentists practice the conversations that matter
articles.description: A University of Rochester collaboration is using an AI-powered virtual patient to help dentists strengthen their communication, build trust and better respond to patients' fears and concerns. For many patients, sitting in a dental chair can be stressful long before treatment begins.

articles.title: In 1979, Researchers Here Said "Put That There." OpenAI Just Called It the Future.
articles.description: When OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, it opened with archival footage from our own Media Room — proof that the most transformative ideas don't expire. On September 3, 2026, OpenAI unveiled GPT-6 Astra, its most powerful model yet, capable of navigating your desktop, writing code, browsing the web, and executing complex workflows on your behalf. The launch video didn't begin with a sleek product demo. It began with 47-year-old footage from a room at MIT. Put that there.

articles.title: Venice Lagoon provides living laboratory for researchers studying climate change
articles.description: Venice really is sinking. Sort of. The home of gondolas, bridges and canals is built across a collection of islands, and the sediments beneath them are gradually compacting, causing the ground to subside. But while the land moves down, climate change is pushing the water up—making the shallow lagoon surrounding the Italian city an increasingly vulnerable environment.

articles.title: Can a full moon really bring bad luck? What about Friday the 13th?
articles.description: Jeffrey Rosenthal was a young professor at the University of Toronto when he discovered he was born on a Friday—though not just any Friday.

articles.title: Unearthing her story: The rise of women archaeologists
articles.description: In a show to kick off a new season, we explore the rise of women archaeologists – and how they are helping to transform our understanding of ancient societies. In the last 30 years, women have come to make up more than half of the profession. At the same time, advances in technology – from DNA analysis to carbon dating – are allowing archaeologists to build a far more accurate picture of the past. And sometimes, that means questioning assumptions that have existed for generations.
